beats.got: nothing new; this is the module title.

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.
beats.got: Agents hand work to each other through shared files. I like the image, but I'm not sure what 'decide' means for agents.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: nothing new; it's homework links and I haven't done the earlier modules' prework.

beats.trigger: **Build** three source-finding agents, each in its source's dialect, and a synthesizer
beats.got: We'll build several agents. 'Dialect' and 'synthesizer' are used before anyone explains them, and nothing here is about people.

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: It's a concrete picture: some agents fetch, others judge. I notice my first worry is who is allowed to see what in Confluence.

beats.trigger: The agent writes the message first and sends only after approval.
beats.got: An agent can act in another system, but only after a human approves. That is a gate I could actually explain to my HR partners and the works council.

beats.trigger: Push back when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I ask the agent for the one thing that unlocks the rest and keep pushing until it stops repeating my own problem back to me. It's useful, but it has no people angle yet.

beats.trigger: Skip any retriever you can't run today.
beats.got: Four sessions, five prompts, 28 minutes. My Confluence or OneDrive may not be connected, and this is the long technical stretch with no word about who does this work.

beats.trigger: Name the doubt; don't fix it here.
beats.got: Three helpers argue from different stances and one synthesis comes out. I'm told I can't yet judge whether it's right, which is honest.

beats.trigger: When do you split, and how?
beats.got: There are two ways to split, and a question I can reason about without a tool.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: The unit is the recurring workflow, like a role's job, not a tool. That is close to how I think about role design.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: Default to one agent. Splitting costs coordination, much like adding a team does.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Split on different access, dialect or stance. Access is the one I recognise: who may see which data, which is my works council and DPO question.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.
beats.got: More agents doesn't mean more rigour. I like the understatement.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Give the synthesizer a framework and it has to choose. Without one it just averages. It also means somebody chose the framework.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: A simple test to apply before building anything multi-agent.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: Separate sessions versus helpers in one session. 'Phase 1/2' and 'bounded return' are jargon I'd have to ask about, and I couldn't repeat the difference.

beats.trigger: **Pick:** Sessions for agents that stay alive; helper agents for in and out.
beats.got: Mostly a repeat of the previous slide, in tool terms.

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.
beats.got: Handoffs lose or silently pick information. That is just like handoffs between my HR partners, and nobody sees the dropped number.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.
beats.got: nothing new; this repeats the earlier point.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in recognisable ways, including sounding confident right before a failure.

beats.trigger: Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.
beats.got: Ask the agent where the fault is before fixing anything. That is a sensible habit.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."
beats.got: Fix the sources, the processing or the boundary, and write the lesson into a rules file. 'Do' to 'propose' is the approval idea again, and a boundary is a human gate.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything off.
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites its own rules file, and I can push back.

beats.trigger: The audit reads how your agents handed work to each other. It does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: The review checks the process but not whether the answer is true. That is a clear, honest limit I can take to leadership.

beats.trigger: *"The planner and the reframer needed to be separate."*
beats.got: I'm expected to argue with the summary. The examples are too specific to my own case to mean much.

beats.trigger: The synthesized briefing's correctness stays an open question today.
beats.got: I should leave today without trusting the output. That is the Nordic understatement I like.

beats.trigger: **Optional move: pressure-test the memory.**
beats.got: nothing new; it's optional homework and I'd skip it.

beats.trigger: Split only where agents can't be one: access, dialect, stance.
beats.got: The takeaway is to split only on access, dialect or stance.

beats.got: nothing new; two more reading links.

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agent risk sits on top of normal security, and I should jot down what matters about our data. The data question is mine, but the text is dense with jargon.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: If agents get access to people data, what is the worst case? This is the question I'd bring to the DPO and the works council.

beats.trigger: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.
beats.got: Keep working on my real problem. Neither suggestion fits my people questions.

take_homes: Start with one agent and split only when access, dialect or stance really differ. Splitting adds coordination cost, like adding a team.
Handoffs are where agent work goes wrong, so I should look at the seams. A review of the process does not tell me the answer is true.
The 'propose, then human approves' gate and the access question are what I'd bring to the DPO and works council before any employee data goes near an agent.

monday.move: Ask my DPO and the works council representative what the rules would be before an agent touches employee data. Then, only if they agree, sketch one single-agent weekly people-metrics summary with a human approval gate.
monday.who: Me, the DPO, and one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday morning for the question; the sketch later in the week
monday.stop_condition: The DPO or the works council says no or not yet. Then I build nothing on employee data.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet. Also, I have no multi-agent need, so one agent is enough.

misconception.why: The module never touched roles or headcount. It said to use one agent where possible, which is a useful caution, but nothing addressed which jobs go, so I still expect agents to replace headcount first.

one_line: Good clear rule on when not to split an agent, and the approval gate was useful. But it's one long technical stretch, and it never says what any of this means for the people doing the work.
